subject: Architecture
title: Tacoma Narrows: The Bridge That Danced
description: A quick win: understand Tacoma Narrows: The Bridge That Danced.

hook.text: In 1940, a suspension bridge in Washington twisted wildly in the wind and tore itself apart on camera.

buildup.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge was nicknamed 'Galloping Gertie' because its deck bounced in even light winds.

discovery.text: Wind created resonant vibrations — the bridge swayed at its natural frequency, amplifying the motion.

twist.text: The only fatality was a dog trapped in a car. Its owner survived by crawling along the heaving deck.

climax.text: The disaster revolutionized bridge engineering. Every suspension bridge since is tested in wind tunnels.

punchline.text: One bridge's death taught every engineer on Earth about wind.

quiz.question: What destroyed the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?
options: An earthquake severed the main cables
Wind-induced resonant vibrations tore it apart
Corrosion weakened the steel support towers

details.summary: The original Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed spectacularly on November 7, 1940, just four months after opening. Wind-induced oscillations caused the bridge deck to twist violently in 40 mph winds, tearing itself apart in a failure that was captured on film and changed bridge engineering forever.
details.whyItMatters: Tacoma Narrows forced engineers to understand aerodynamic forces on bridges. Every suspension bridge designed since then includes wind tunnel testing and aerodynamic shaping.
takeaways: Collapsed November 7, 1940, just four months after opening
Wind-induced oscillations twisted the deck apart in 40 mph winds
The failure revolutionized bridge aerodynamic engineering

faq.question: What caused the Tacoma Narrows Bridge to collapse?
faq.answer: The thin, flat deck acted like an airplane wing, catching wind that induced torsional flutter — a self-reinforcing oscillation. The bridge deck twisted more and more violently until the cables snapped. The failure is technically aeroelastic flutter, not simple resonance as often claimed.

faq.question: Were there any casualties?
faq.answer: Only one casualty — a cocker spaniel named Tubby who was too frightened to leave an abandoned car. The bridge had been closed to traffic due to the swaying. The last person on the bridge, reporter Leonard Coatsworth, crawled to safety just before the span fell.
